title: Indexing the Internet
description: Understand how a search engine works — web crawling, inverted indexes, TF-IDF relevance scoring, PageRank, and distributed query processing.

segments.text: Google processes over eight billion searches per day across billions of web pages. In under half a second. Let's design the system that makes searching the entire internet feel instant.

First, you need the data. Web crawlers start from seed URLs, download pages, extract links, and follow them. It's a massive breadth-first traversal of the web graph. Politeness policies prevent overwhelming any single site.

Crawlers encounter duplicates constantly. The same page at different URLs, mirror sites, near-identical content. URL deduplication uses a bloom filter for speed. Content deduplication uses simhash to detect near-duplicate pages efficiently.

The inverted index is the heart of search. For every word, it stores a list of documents containing that word along with positions. Searching for 'distributed systems' means intersecting the posting lists for 'distributed' and 'systems.'
The inverted index returns thousands of matching documents. But the user wants the ten most relevant. How do you decide which documents are most relevant to a query?
segments.thought_prompt: What signals would you use to rank search results by relevance?

segments.text: TF-IDF scores relevance. Term Frequency measures how often a word appears in a document. Inverse Document Frequency penalizes common words like 'the.' A document where 'distributed' appears frequently but 'the' is common scores high for 'distributed.'

But content relevance isn't enough. PageRank measures page authority by counting and weighting incoming links. A page linked by many authoritative pages is itself authoritative. It's a recursive definition solved by iterating until values converge.

A query hits the search system. It's parsed, spell-corrected, and expanded with synonyms. Then the index is queried, results are scored combining TF-IDF, PageRank, and hundreds of other signals. Top results are returned in milliseconds.

The index is far too large for one machine. It's sharded across thousands of servers. Each shard holds a portion of the index. A query is broadcast to all shards in parallel, each returns its top results, and a coordinator merges and re-ranks them.
Here's a tension. Building an index over billions of pages takes time. But news breaks every second, and users expect fresh results. How do you keep the index current?
segments.thought_prompt: How would you balance index freshness with the cost of re-crawling and re-indexing billions of pages?

segments.text: The solution is tiered indexing. A small real-time index handles breaking news and frequently changing pages. A larger batch index covers the broader web, rebuilt periodically. Query results merge from both tiers, balancing freshness with coverage.

A search engine is a pipeline: crawl the web, deduplicate, build an inverted index, score with TF-IDF and PageRank, shard the index across thousands of machines, and process queries in parallel. Simple to describe, monumental to build at scale.
